Triggers.value: Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs

vignette:
Mark, a 33-year-old graphic designer, traces the start of it all back to a single evening ten months ago. He was walking home from a late work session, cutting through a downtown square bustling with post-concert crowds. It was after midnight, the streetlights casting long, distorted shadows. He remembers the sudden screech of tires and the abrupt stop of a dark, boxy sedan right beside him. Before he could fully register the make or model, the doors flew open and he was surrounded. In the chaos of shouting and shoving from the crowd, he was slammed against a brick wall, his face pressed into the cold, gritty surface. He felt the unmistakable pressure of a gun barrel at the base of his skull. The world narrowed to that single point of contact, the metallic smell of the weapon, and the blinding flashes of disorientation under the streetlights. It was a case of mistaken identity, sorted out within an hour at the precinct, but the damage was already done.

In the weeks that followed, the city he had always loved began to feel like a landscape of threats. His work required him to be downtown, but the once-energizing hum of crowds now felt suffocating, a chaotic mass where danger could erupt at any moment. He started taking convoluted routes to his office, adding forty minutes to his commute just to avoid the busier squares. He found himself cataloging every dark-coloured sedan he saw, his breath catching in his throat whenever one slowed down nearby. He was certain that another mistake was imminent, that his face was now somehow marked for disaster. The nights became the worst part. Waking up in the pitch-black of his bedroom would trigger a jolt of pure terror, his heart hammering against his ribs as he was plunged back into the memory of that moment by the wall.

To manage this, Mark developed a set of rigid, private rituals. He began drinking a few glasses of whiskey each night, the only thing that seemed to quiet the relentless internal alarm bell long enough for him to fall asleep. What started as a tool for sleep soon became a crutch for getting through the day. He'd have a drink before facing his commute, another as soon as he got home. His avoidance became more pronounced. A police drama on television would send him scrambling for the remote. If he saw an officer on the street, he would immediately cross to the other side, his gaze fixed on the pavement, sometimes instinctively bringing his hands up to shield his face as if to make himself invisible.

His ex-wife, Emily, had tried to be patient. She couldn't understand his visceral reactions-the way he'd flinch at the sight of a uniform, or his flat-out refusal to go to any restaurant or event that might be crowded. His world had shrunk, and he was pulling her into its claustrophobic confines. The drinking, the secrecy, the constant, humming tension-it created a chasm between them that eventually became too wide to cross. They divorced six months ago. Since then, Mark's isolation has deepened. His freelance work has dried up as he struggles to focus, his creativity drowned out by a persistent sense of dread.

The decision to seek therapy came after a particularly humiliating incident last week. He was walking to the grocery store when he saw a police car parked ahead. A wave of panic so intense it made him dizzy washed over him. He ducked into an alleyway, crouching behind a dumpster and covering his face with his hands, gasping for air. He stayed there for ten minutes, shaking, long after the car had driven away. The shame of that moment, of being a grown man hiding from the world in broad daylight, was the final straw. Mark now sits in the therapist's office, articulating a quiet, desperate hope: to reclaim his life from a fear that has consumed everything, and to one day be able to simply walk through his own city, in the dark, without feeling like he is about to die.
